Three-stage integrated co-digestion of pig manure and rice straw combined 
with biogas slurry reflux: Performance and application evaluation
Kaitao Peng a, Min Sun b, Wei Zeng b, Qi Zhang a, Yunpu Wang a, Shuyu Xiang a, Yuhuan Liu a,*,  
Xian Cui a,*
a State Key Laboratory of Food Science and Resources, Engineering Research Center for Biomass Conversion, Ministry of Education, Nanchang University, Nanchang,

H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• A three-stage integrated co-digestion 
(TSAD) process was developed.
• TSAD enriched the stage-specific func­
tional flora by spatial segregation.
• TSAD enabled the reduction of biogas 
slurry emissions via biogas slurry reflux.
• TSAD enhanced processing capacity and 
reduced the consumption of clean 
water.
• HRT = 20 d, TSAD maintained efficient 
and stable methane production within 
120 days.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Biogas slurry reduction
Agricultural waste
Microbial community
High organic loading rate
A B S T R A C T
To address the challenges associated with the large-scale production and difficult disposal of biogas slurry in 
conventional high-solid anaerobic digestion, this study developed a three-stage integrated co-digestion (TSAD) 
process integrated with biogas slurry reflux (BSR), and assessed its feasibility for stable semi-continuous oper­
ation over a 120-day period. Results demonstrate that TSAD enables targeted enrichment among functional 
microbial communities—achieved through spatially segregated operational stages: aerobic hydrolysis, micro­
aerobic acidification, and anaerobic methanogenesis. Under an appropriate hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 20 
days, the system achieved sustained high biogas production stability (with a final methane yield of 218 mL/g 
COD). Crucially, relying on the comprehensive strategy of high-solid feedstock, staged separation and BSR, it 
enhanced overall treatment efficiency by approximately 2.8-fold relative to conventional single-stage system, 
while reducing daily water consumption per unit substrate by 83.3 %, thereby substantially mitigating slurry 
emission. In contrast, reducing the HRT to 10 days boosted short-term biogas production, but also enhanced the 
mobilization of copper and zinc into the liquid phase and caused rapid accumulation of ammonia nitrogen (up to 
4855.1 mg/L) during prolonged operation, ultimately increasing the risk of process instability and potential 
system failure. These findings provide a theoretical basis for achieving process optimization through staged

1. Introduction
To achieve the goals of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, pro­
moting the replacement of fossil fuels with clean energy has become a 
global consensus (Zhang and You, 2023). Among various strategies, 
efficient utilization of biomass waste represents a critical pathway 
(Zhang et al., 2026). Anaerobic digestion (AD), as a mature technology 
for biomass treatment, enables the conversion of organic matter into 
clean biogas through microbial synergism. This process offers dual 
benefits—effective waste management and renewable energy produc­
tion, and plays a significant role in advancing carbon emission re­
ductions (Awodun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2019).
As the country with the fastest expansion of AD, China had approx­
imately 100,000 industrial digesters and a total number of about 39.1 
million digestion tanks by 2020 (Ni, 2024; Zheng et al., 2020). However, 
in recent years, it has seen stagnation or even negative growth in project 
expansion in certain regions (Ni, 2024). Multiple factors contribute to 
this trend, among which the difficulty in the utilization of biogas slurry 
(BS) is widely recognized as the most critical bottleneck constraining the 
sustainable development of biogas projects (Yang et al., 2019; Zeng 
et al., 2022). As the primary by-product of AD, BS is rich in organic 
matter and essential nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus; how­
ever, it may also contain potential contaminants including heavy metals 
and antibiotic residues (Liu et al., 2021). Although stringent emission 
standards have been established, compliance requires complex pre­
treatment procedures and substantial financial investment (Zhang et al., 
2020). More critically, even after meeting regulatory requirements, 
large land areas are still needed for safe application, which many farms 
lack due to limited surrounding arable land (Sheets et al., 2015). 
Furthermore, studies indicate that labor costs associated with applying 
BS and biogas residue are approximately ten times higher than those for 
chemical fertilizers, significantly reducing farmers’ willingness to utilize 
these materials (Li et al., 2021), which further aggravates the dilemma 
of BS utilization. These factors collectively contributing to the prevalent 
phenomenon of “prioritizing construction over operation” in biogas 
projects and resulting in insufficient resource utilization.
In response to these challenges, reduction and resource-oriented 
utilization of BS have emerged as key technical directions for the 
transformation and upgrading of biogas systems. Currently, various 
approaches are being explored to minimize BS generation and enhance 
its value. Biogas slurry reflux (BSR) technology facilitates the reuse of 
organic matter and functional microorganisms by returning a portion of 
the BS back into the digester (Li et al., 2023). This strategy not only 
reduces overall BS emission but also enhances methane (CH4) produc­
tion and system stability (Li et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2023). Research by Li 
et al. demonstrates that BSR promotes the establishment of specialized 
microbial communities, accelerates organic hydrolysis and hydrogen 
(H2) production, and delivers both environmental and economic ad­
vantages (Li et al., 2020). Nevertheless, conventional single-stage 
anaerobic digestion (SSAD) processes face inherent limitations: under 
high organic loading rates (OLR), the rates of hydrolysis/acidification 
and methanogenesis become mismatched, resulting in a long hydraulic 
retention time (HRT, typically 20–50 days) for the system (Mahdy et al., 
2019; Xu et al., 2023), which is contradictable with the BS reduction 
requirements.
Owing to the inherent limitations of SSAD systems, two-stage AD 
configurations and various pretreatment strategies—including aerobic 
and microaerobic pretreatment, thermal extrusion, and others—have 
been widely investigated to mitigate process inhibition and enhance 
biogas yield (Ning et al., 2023; Oluwagbotemi Fasheun et al., 2024; 
Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2016; You et al., 2024). Nevertheless, these 
approaches remain susceptible to thermodynamic inefficiencies and 
potential secondary environmental impacts. Notably, conventional two- 
stage systems typically integrate hydrolysis and acidogenesis within a 
single upstream reactor. Given the substantial physiological disparities 
(e.g., optimal pH) between hydrolytic enzymes and acidogenic bacteria, 
such spatial co-location engenders kinetic incompatibilities, thereby 
compromising biochemical conversion efficiency at the initial stage 
(Tang et al., 2023).
To overcome these constraints, this study introduces a novel three- 
stage integrated process (TSAD): “aerobic/microaerobic/anaerobic co- 
digestion combined with BSR.” The process aims to decouple AD into 
three functionally distinct and spatially separated stages, including hy­
drolysis, acidogenesis, and methanogenesis, thereby eliminating kinetic 
interference and enabling precise optimization of ecological niches for 
each functional microbial consortium. Concurrently, combined with 
BSR, it will achieve the goal of reducing slurry emissions while sus­
taining high OLR and operational stability. This work will not only offer 
a new perspective to overcome the long-standing hydrolysis–acido­
genesis coupling bottleneck, but also establishes a robust theoretical and 
technical foundation for advancing next-generation agricultural waste 
treatment technologies characterized by high conversion efficiency and 
low emission.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum and substrate
Pig manure (PM) used in the experiment was collected from a large- 
scale swine farm in Pingxiang, Jiangxi, China. After manual screening to 
remove large soil particles and animal hair, the material was passed 
through a 60-mesh sieve (particle size < 425 μm) and stored at 4℃ for 
subsequent use. Rice straw (RS) was sourced from Nanchang, Jiangxi, 
China. Following mechanical crushing, it was stored through a 60-mesh 
sieve. The main physicochemical characteristics of RS and PM are pre­
sented in Table 1.
The inoculum for the acidification reactor was derived from acetic 
acid bacterial residue generated during vinegar brewing. A 20-gram 
sample was sealed in a 100-mesh nylon bag and subjected to pre- 
adaptation cultivation using effluent from the hydrolysis tank until 
stable performance was achieved. The inoculum for the methanogenic 
reactor was obtained from a long-term AD system in Nanchang, where 
RS served as the primary substrate. Prior to use, it underwent pre- 
acclimation with effluent from the acidification reactor.

2.2. Equipment description
The schematic designs of the TSAD and SSAD systems are presented 
in Fig. 1. The TSAD system comprises an aerobic hydrolysis tank (TR1, 
with a total volume of 14 L and an effective volume of 3 L), followed by a 
microaerobic acidizing tank (TR2, 1.5 L total volume, 1 L effective 
volume), and an anaerobic CH4-producing tank (TR3, total volume of 6 
L, effective volume of 5 L). Within TR1, a sieve plate lined with 500- 
mesh gauze was divided the tank into two functional zones: an upper 
material storage zone with top-space pressure equalization (approxi­
mately 9 L), and a lower hydrolysis liquid collection zone (with a total 
volume of 5 L and an effective volume of 3 L). The SSAD system consists 
of a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) (SR, total volume was 5 L, 
effective volume was 4 L). All reactors are equipped with external 
circulating water jacket layers for temperature control, maintained at 
37℃ using a thermostatic water bath (SHZ-B, China Boxun Medical 
Biological Instrument Co., LTD). Gas outlets from SR, TR2 and TR3 are 
connected to gas collection bags, and these reactors are fitted with 
intermittent stirring devices operating at 20 rpm, programmed to stir for 
5 min at 8-hour intervals. The material transfer between reactors is 
achieved through peristaltic pumps.

thoroughly mixed feedstock was put into the upper section of the sieve

of working followed by 5 min of stopping—with a volumetric airflow 
rate of 2000 mL-air/min during operation. When liquid–solid separation 
was required, the pressure relief valve was opened to equalize the in­
ternal pressure. Under gravitational force, the hydrolyzed liquid flowed 
along the 15◦inclined base of the tank toward the outlet and was then 
transferred to TR2 using a peristaltic pump. Upon completion of acidi­
fication, the treated material was pumped into TR3 for further pro­
cessing. Finally, the effluent from TR3 was combined with fresh 
feedstock and recirculated back to TR1, thereby achieving the recycling 
of liquid slurry. The SSAD system continuously fed in and out in 
accordance with the conventional CSTR mode.
To ensure stable system operation, the daily feed compositions for 
each reactor in the TSAD system are specified as follows: The daily 
feedstock for TR1 consisted of a mixture of PM and RS at a mass ratio of 
1:1, with liquid slurry recirculated from TR3, and supplementary 
distilled water. More details on the reflux liquid slurry are provided in 
the supplementary materials (see Supplementary Materials). The daily 
feed to TR2 comprised two components: (i) the hydrolysate obtained by 
centrifugation (5,000 rpm) of the equal amount of mixture discharged 
from the upper part of TR1 (with a liquid separation rate of approxi­
mately 40 %); and (ii) the residual portion of the hydrolysate obtained 
from the lower-layer slurry of TR1 following depressurization. The daily 
feed of TR3 was the complete effluent from TR2. The SSAD system 
employed an identical ratio of PM to RS as TR1 but substituted distilled 
water for BS and maintained the TS concentration at 6 % to mitigate 
potential ammonia inhibition (Wijesinghe et al., 2021).
2.3.2. Comparative experiments of SSAD and TSAD system under different 
HRTs
Throughout the entire experimental period, the total HRT was kept 
consistent both the TSAD and SSAD systems. Based on prior research 
findings (Xiang et al., 2022), the experiment was divided into multiple 
HRT stages. The experiments involving varying HRTs were conducted 
sequentially: for each HRT, the system was operated continuously until 
steady-state conditions (at least 2 to 3 HRTs), after which the system was 
transitioned to the next designated HRT. The specific feed parameters of 
each reactor in the SSAD and TSAD systems at different HRTs are shown 
in Table 2.
2.3.3. Long-term operational stability test
Following the comparative HRT experiment, a 120-day continuous 
operation test was conducted to assess the long-term operational sta­
bility of the two systems. Specifically, the SSAD system was operated at 
an HRT of 30 days, whereas the TSAD system was evaluated under two 
distinct HRT conditions—20 days and 10 days.
2.4. Sampling and chemical analysis
During the HRT comparison experiment, digested samples were 
collected daily from the sampling port of each reactor. For the long-term 
stability experiment, samples were obtained at three critical time points: 
system startup (Day 0), mid-operation (Day 60), and end-of-operation 
(Day 120). Measurement of TS, VS, TC, TOC, volatile fatty acids 
(VFAs), soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD), total ammonia ni­
trogen (TAN), and lignocellulosic components (including lignin, cellu­
lose, and hemicellulose) was analyzed referring to the previous report 
(Xiang et al., 2022).
Generated biogas was collected using gas collection bags, and the 
total volume was recorded using a wet gas flowmeter (LMF-1, Jinzhiye 
Instrument & Equipment Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). The concentrations 
of CH4 and carbon dioxide (CO2) in the biogas were analyzed using a 
portable biogas analyzer (Biogas 5000, Geotech, UK).
The concentrations of heavy metals, including Copper (Cu) and Zinc 
(Zn), in both liquid and solid fraction of the effluent were determined by 
inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, 
OPTIMA 8000, PerkinElmer, USA).
2.5. Microbial structure analysis
The microbial diversity of fungi and bacteria in TR1, bacteria and 
archaea in TR2 and archaea in TR3 were measured. Sequencing was 
conducted by Shanghai Majorbio Technology Co., Ltd. The specific 
methods are referred to in previous report (Xiang et al., 2022). Primers 
for amplifying the gene were as follows: ITS1F (5′-CTTGGTCATTTA­
GAGGAAGTAA-3′) and ITS2R (5′-GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC-3′) were 
used to amplify the ITS1 region of the fungal ITF gene. The V3-V4 region

GAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). The 
V4-V5 regions of archaea were amplified using 524F10extF (5′-TGY­

2.6. Carbon flow analysis
Carbon flow analysis was calculated based on the total mass, TS, TC 
and TOC change recorded during the experiment. The detailed calcu­
lation method is shown in the supplementary materials (see 
Supplementary Materials).
2.7. Statistics
The obtained data were organized using Microsoft Excel 2016. 
Graphs were plotted using Origin 2024. The data are expressed as means 
± standard deviations (M ± SD), based on at least three technical rep­
licates per sample. The sequencing results were analyzed in the Majorbio 
Cloud Platform (https://www.majorbio.com). The Circos map of mi­
crobial community structure was drawn through the online platform 
(https://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/tableviewer/visualize/) based on the method 
of (Krzywinski et al., 2009). No hypothesis testing (e.g., ANOVA) was 
performed due to the absence of biological replicates (i.e., single reactor 
sequential operation).

Under these conditions, the VS/TS ratio was 75.2 %, indicating rela­

of volatile solids and contributes to system stability. In contrast, in the 
SSAD system, reducing the HRT from 30 days to 10 days resulted in 
insufficient utilization of readily degradable organic matter, as evi­
denced by declining TS and VS degradation rates and an increase in the

mg/g to 12 mg/g, suggesting that a substantial portion of TOC remained 
unconverted in the solid fraction. Conversely, in the TSAD system with 
an HRT of 4 days in the aerobic hydrolysis stage, although TC and TOC 
levels in the solid phase increased due to reduced carbon transfer, the 
TOC proportion in the liquid slurry reached 94.7 %. This indicates that 
nearly all organic carbon was successfully transferred into the liquid 
phase in bioavailable forms, thereby providing abundant substrate for 
the subsequent anaerobic digestion stage. This outcome highlights a 
marked improvement over the limited carbon utilization observed in the 
SSAD system.

findings are consistent with those reported by (Rennuit et al., 2018), 
confirming that aerobic pretreatment effectively improves the bio­

The lignocellulose degradation performance in the SSAD system and 
aerobic hydrolysis stages of TSAD system are illustrated Fig. 3d-3f. The 
results show that, under varying HRT conditions, TR1 (representing the 
TSAD system) achieves higher degradation rates of cellulose, hemicel­
lulose, and lignin compared to SR (SSAD), with only 40 % of the treat­
ment time required. Notably, at an HRT of 10 days, TR1 exhibited 
degradation rate enhancements of 35.2 %, 46.4 %, and 71.0 % for cel­
lulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, respectively, relative to SR. These re­
sults underscore the superior short-term efficiency of aerobic hydrolysis 
in breaking down recalcitrant lignocellulosic components, thereby 
ensuring a sufficient supply of bioavailable substrates for the subsequent 
CH4 production phase. This finding aligns with the results reported by 
Zhang et al., 2019a, who demonstrated that aerobic hydrolysis markedly 
disrupted the lignin structure across all anatomical components of corn 
stalks, thereby increasing the specific CH4 yield (per unit volatile solids) 
by 8–35.02 % relative to the untreated control and substantially 
reducing the overall fermentation duration.
3.1.2. Microaerobic acidification stage of TSAD versus SSAD
With respect to liquid-phase metabolites, the microaerobic acidifi­
cation reactor has demonstrated an active regulatory capability for 
dissolved organic matter. When the HRT of the acidification stage is 
maintained at 3 days, the effluent VFA concentration (2879 mg/L) is 
lower than that of the influent (3239 mg/L), indicating net VFA con­
sumption (Fig. 2c). However, when the HRT is reduced to 1 day, the 
reactor actively enriches VFAs to a concentration of 11,987 mg/L—1.32 
times higher than the influent—demonstrating its adaptive metabolic 
control. This flexible regulatory capability ensures the provision of 
substrates with appropriate concentration and optimized composition 
for the subsequent methanogenic stage, which is fundamentally 
different from the malignant accumulation of VFAs in the SSAD system.
The distinction between the two systems becomes even more pro­
nounced in terms of operational conditions and product profiles. While 
the SSAD system was accumulating VFAs, it was accompanied by the 
decrease of CH4 content to 45.7 % and system fluctuations, which re­
flected the inherent contradiction that hydrolysis, acidification and CH4 
production inhibited each other in the same space (Yang et al., 2023). In 
contrast, in the microaerobic acidification stage of the TSAD system, 
shortening the HRT from 3 to 1 day leads to enhanced VFAs concen­
tration, a corresponding decrease in system pH from 6.76 to 5.89, and an 
notable increase in volume biogas production rate (Fig. 2d), which may 
be attributed to the generation of CO2 and H2 during acidogenesis and 
acetogenesis (Al-Rubaye et al., 2020; Gujer and Zehnder, 1983; Parra- 
Orobio et al., 2020). Moreover, the CH4 production observed during 
this stage is likely due to the introduction of a limited population of 
methanogenic archaea via BSR (as detailed in Section 3.2), while the low 
CH4 content may be associated with inhibitory effects caused by acid 
accumulation under low HRT conditions (Dzofou Ngoumelah et al., 
2023; Guo et al., 2025; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018).
3.1.3. Anaerobic methanogenic stage of TSAD versus SSAD
The anaerobic methanogenic stage, serving as the final phase of the 
TSAD system, exhibits high substrate conversion efficiency and superior 
biogas quality. When the HRT was reduced from 10 to 5 days, the vol­
ume biogas production rate increased from 522 mL/L/d to 1665 mL/L/ 
d. The combined content of CH4 and CO2 in the biogas consistently 
exceeded 97.5 % (Fig. 2f), thereby reducing the difficulty of subsequent 
biogas purification. Notably, as the HRT decreased from 15 to 5 days, 
the CH4 content rose from 52.5 % to 61.9 %, whereas the CO2 content 
declined from 45.5 % to 37.2 %. This phenomenon may be attributed to 
the change in the archaeal community structure during this stage (see 
Section 3.2 for details). This shift may be attributed to enhanced H2 
production driven by elevated organic acid concentrations in the feed, 
which promotes the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway (Zhu 
et al., 2020, Zhu et al., 2019), resulting in increased CH4 formation 
through CO2 consumption. In contrast, the SSAD system achieved a 
volume biogas production rate of 401.2 mL/L/d at an HRT of 30 days, 
with a CH4 content of approximately 55.2 %. Although the volume 
biogas production rate increased to 904.9 mL/L/d when the HRT was 
reduced to 10 days, the CH4 content dropped markedly to 45.7 %, 
indicating challenges in maintaining stable biogas composition under 
higher OLR. Furthermore, the anaerobic methanogenic stage of TSAD 
system achieved removal efficiencies of 73.1 %, 88.1 %, 58.7 %, and 
82.6 % for sCOD, VFAs, TC, and TOC, respectively (Fig. 2e). Despite the 
significantly shortened HRT, the TSAD system did not impose a sub­
stantial burden on subsequent treatment processes, demonstrating su­
perior operational flexibility and conversion efficiency compared to the 
SSAD configuration.
3.2. Functional response of microbial community structure to TSAD 
system
The relative abundances of different bacterial communities of 
different stages at the genus level were shown in Fig. 4. During the 
hydrolysis stage, the fungal community was predominantly composed of 
Candida, Geotrichum, and Trichosporon. Notably, the relative abundance 
of Candida increased by 17-fold (from 2.34 % to 42.3 %) under short 
HRT conditions (Fig. 4a). Previous studies have demonstrated that 
Candida plays a pivotal role in the rapid degradation of lignocellulosic 
materials (Li et al., 2017a), which aligns with the observed high ligno­
cellulose degradation efficiency during this stage (Fig. 3d-3f). Within the 
bacterial community, hydrolytic and acidogenic genera such as Rumi­
nofilibacter, Prevotella, Ruminiclostridium, and Prevotellaceae_UCG-001 
were dominant (Fig. 4b). Prevotella and Prevotellaceae_UCG-001 
belong to the family Prevotellaceae, which has been reported to facili­
tate the hydrolysis and acidification of straw substrates (Lazuka et al., 
2015; Jose et al., 2017). Ruminofilibacter and Ruminiclostridium are 
recognized as key functional microorganisms involved in the conversion 
of carbohydrates into small-molecule organic acids (Azman et al., 2015;

3.3. Analysis of carbon flow
This study conducted a comparative analysis of carbon flow in SSAD 
and TSAD systems (Fig. 5), to evaluate resource utilization and reduc­
tion efficiency across different processes. In the SSAD process, as HRT 
decreased from 30 to 10 days, the proportion of gaseous carbon (CH4 
and CO2) converted declined, while the fraction of liquid carbon (in BS) 
increased. This indicates reduced biogas production efficiency and a 
higher burden on downstream BS treatment. Such phenomenon is 
commonly observed in conventional SSAD system, particularly under 
shortened HRTs, the slow-growing methanogens are prone to washout, 
leading to incomplete VFA consumption and consequent carbon accu­
mulation in the liquid phase (Mao et al., 2015). In contrast, in the TSAD 
process, as the total HRT was shortened from 30 days to 10 days, the 
carbon distribution in the hydrolysis stage changed: the proportion of 
carbon lost as fugitive gas decreased from 34.6 % to 17.4 %, whereas the 
carbon content in the hydrolysate increased from 10.0 % to 18.7 %. This 
shift suggests enhanced transfer of carbon from volatile forms into the 
liquid phase, thereby providing more available substrates for subsequent 
stages. Under a 10-day HRT, the total carbon entering the methano­
genesis stage increased by 0.9 times compared to the 30-day condition. 
Ultimately, 6.7 % of the initial carbon was converted into CH4, resulting 
in a CH4 production 2.6 times higher than that under prolonged HRT. 
Although the CH4 conversion efficiency of the TSAD system at a 10-day 
HRT was 63 % lower than that of the SSAD system at 30 days, its CH4 
production rate per unit time was substantially improved, with com­
parable residual carbon levels in solid and liquid phases. The observed 
difference primarily arises from aerobic carbon loss during the 
hydrolysis stage—specifically, partial oxidation of organic carbon to 
CO2 via aerobic microbial respiration. Nevertheless, extant literature 
indicates that aerobic pretreatment or microaerobic hydrolysis, despite 
modest organic carbon losses, significantly accelerates both hydrolytic 
enzyme synthesis and the depolymerization of recalcitrant biopolymers 
(Huili˜nir et al., 2023). Thus, this carbon “input” has resulted in an 
enhancement of the overall processing throughput and system stability, 
highlighting the process's comprehensive performance advantages 
under high loading conditions.
3.4. Potential and limitations of TSAD process
The concentration of TAN and heavy metal (Cu and Zn), biogas 
production potential during the long-term operation of the SSAD and 
TSAD systems are presented in Table 3.
The accumulation of ammonia nitrogen constitutes a critical limiting 
factor for the long-term stable operation of AD systems (Chen et al., 
2015; Huang et al., 2018). In the SSAD system operated at an HRT of 30 
days, the TAN concentration increased from 494.4 mg/L on Day 0 to 
2694.4 mg/L on Day 120, while CH4 yield rose steadily from 79.7 mL/g 
COD to 95.7 mL/g COD—indicating robust process stability. By contrast, 
in the TSAD system operated at an HRT of 20 days over 120 days, TAN 
accumulated to 3290.4 mg/L; yet the system sustained a high volumetric 
biogas production rate of 589 mL/L/d, with CH4 content remaining 
stable at 55.6 %. Concurrently, the specific CH4 yield (based on COD) 
increased from 179.8 mL/g COD on Day 0 to 236.4 mL/g COD on Day 
60, and remained elevated at 218.0 mL/g COD on Day 120—further 
confirming operational resilience under moderate ammonia stress. This 
might be attributed to progressive microbial adaptation to elevated 
ammonia concentrations, indicating that the TSAD system exhibits 
certain ammonia tolerance within this operational load range. As 
documented in prior literature, TAN concentrations exceeding 3000 
mg/L markedly enhance ammonium ion toxicity independent of pH, 
thereby compromising process stability (Wu et al., 2016). In this study, 
when the HRT was further reduced to 10 days, TAN in the TSAD system 
rose to 3081.2 mg/L after 60 days and escalated to 4855.1 mg/L after 
120 days. Concurrently, the biogas production rate declined 
sharply—from 1423 mL/L/d to 535 mL/L/d—and CH4 content fell 
below 40 %, and the CH4 yield dropped precipitously from 248.3 mL/g

The distribution of heavy metals in the system effluent warrants 
careful consideration. In this study, Cu and Zn were predominantly 
retained in the solid residue of both the SSAD and TSAD systems, 
consistent with prior findings attributing heavy metal immobilization to 
complexation and adsorption onto organic matter (Carliell-Marquet and 
Wheatley, 2002). Notably, the concentrations of Cu and Zn in both the 
solid residue and liquid slurry of the TSAD system exceeded those 
observed in the SSAD system. This trend aligns with Ni et al.’s findings 
on enhanced heavy metal accumulation during anaerobic digestion 
when BS is recirculated (Ni et al., 2017). Moreover, shortening the HRT 
from 20 to 10 days led to increased Cu and Zn concentrations in the 
liquid slurry of the TSAD system. This increase is likely attributable to 
elevated hydraulic shear stress under higher OLRs. In anaerobic sludge, 
heavy metals are typically sequestered within extracellular polymeric 
substances (EPS) and associated with microbial flocs; however, height­
ened shear forces can compromise floc integrity and induce EPS disin­
tegration, thereby mobilizing previously bound metal ions into the 
aqueous phase (Li et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2016). Such metal release 
may impair subsequent solid–liquid separation efficiency and influence 
downstream digestate management. The above results suggest that the 
TSAD effluent—characterized by comparatively higher heavy metal 
loads—may present non-negligible environmental risks, particularly 
upon land application. Consequently, routine monitoring of heavy metal 
concentrations in system effluents is recommended in operational 
practice, accompanied by systematic evaluation of potential impacts on 
soil quality and crop safety.
From a technical and economic standpoint, when the reactor volume 
is normalized to 1 m3, the TSAD process demonstrates enhanced pro­
cessing capacity relative to SSAD due to its integrated strategy of high 
solid feeding, staged separation and BSR (Table 4). Specifically, at an 
HRT of 20 days, the TSAD system achieved a daily organic loading rate 
of 5.30 kg, whereas the SSAD system attained only 1.89 kg/day at an 
HRT of 30 days, representing a 2.8-fold improvement in processing ca­
pacity. This enhancement is primarily attributable to the integrated 
aerobic hydrolysis stage in TSAD, which facilitates effective pretreat­
ment of feedstock, thereby increasing substrate biodegradability alle­
viates the hydrolytic bottleneck inherent in conventional single-stage 
digestion. As a result, the system achieves stable operation at higher 
OLRs—even under shortened HRTs (Vanegas and Bartlett, 2013). 
Furthermore, under a TS concentration of 15 % in the feed, the TSAD 
process reduced clean water demand: at an HRT of 20 days, its daily 
water consumption per unit substrate was merely 8.47 L, corresponding 
to an 83.3 % reduction compared with the SSAD system (18.11 L/day at 
an HRT of 30 days). This pronounced reduction in BS emission volume 
not only lowers downstream dewatering and transport costs but also 
mitigates associated environmental burdens. Meanwhile, under iden­
tical HRT conditions, the TSAD system generated 8.14 kg/day of biogas 
residue (calculated based on a moisture content of 70 %), approximately 
2.6 times the residue output of the SSAD system (3.08 kg/day), indi­
cating that this process is better suited to regions with adequate land 
availability for residue disposal or well-established downstream residue 
treatment and valorization infrastructure, thereby facilitating the safe 
and efficient conversion of digested residue into organic fertilizers or 
other value-added products.
To further elucidate the technical positioning and novelty of the 
TSAD process, a systematic performance comparison was conducted 
against representative AD configurations widely reported in recent 
literature (Table 5). Specifically, relative to the two-phase hyper­
thermophilic–mesophilic co-digestion process reported by Chen et al. 
(2021) (HRT = 30 days; CH4 yield = 510 mL/g VS), the TSAD process 
achieves a 33 % reduction in HRT while enabling more precise enrich­
ment of functional microbial communities—facilitated by spatial sepa­
ration of hydrolysis and acidification zones—and avoids the energy 
losses from the switching between hyperthermophilic and mesophilic 
conditions. In comparison with the two-phase system with double thin- 
slurry reflux described by Janesch et al. (2025) (HRT = 20 days; CH4 
yield = 260 mL/g COD), the TSAD process exhibits a marginally lower 
CH4 yield but demonstrates distinct advantages in volumetric organic 
loading capacity and reduction of digestate volume emissions.

In summary, the TSAD process offers compelling advantages in terms 
of processing capacity, water conservation, and reduction of BS, making 
it particularly suitable for centralized agricultural waste treatment fa­
cilities with high resource recovery objectives. Its optimal deployment 
hinges on the rational selection of HRT to mitigate ammonia inhibition

4. Conclusion
The operational performance of TSAD process under varying HRTs 
were systematically evaluated. Results demonstrated that TSAD enabled 
directional enrichment of functional microbial communities by physi­
cally separating the hydrolysis, acidogenesis and methanogenesis stages, 
thereby enhancing its resilience to high OLRs. Under an HRT of 10 days, 
the system achieved a volume biogas production rate of 1665 mL/L/ 
d with a CH4 content of 61.9 %, indicating excellent short-term biogas 
production potential. Nevertheless, prolonged operation (120 days) at 
this HRT induced progressive accumulation of TAN (4855.1 mg/L), 
causing pronounced inhibition of methanogenic activity. Concurrently, 
the residual concentrations of heavy metals (Cu and Zn) increased in the 
liquid phase, thereby elevating environmental risk. In contrast, under an 
HRT of 20 days, the system achieved stable and efficient biogas pro­
duction performance over the same 120-day period. By integrating high- 
solid feedstock, staged separation and BSR, it delivered a processing 
capacity approximately 2.8-fold higher than the traditional SSAD pro­
cess, while reducing specific water consumption per unit substrate by 
83.3 %, thereby effectively achieving the reduction of BS emission. 
These findings demonstrate that the TSAD system’s long-term opera­
tional stability necessitates careful HRT selection coupled with heavy 
metal immobilization and targeted ammonia nitrogen removal from 
recirculated slurry, so as to turn potential risks into resource recovery 
opportunities.
